clinicalPearls: Acute radiation syndrome follows a high, acute whole-body or large partial-body dose of penetrating ionising radiation, as in criticality accidents or radiological incidents
It classically evolves through a prodromal phase (nausea, vomiting, malaise), a latent phase, a manifest illness phase and then either recovery or death
The speed of onset of vomiting is a useful early guide to dose severity, with earlier vomiting indicating higher exposure
Recognised dose-dependent sub-syndromes affect the bone marrow (haematopoietic), the gastrointestinal tract, and at very high doses the cardiovascular and central nervous systems
Serial lymphocyte counts over the first day or two are a practical biological indicator of the dose received and prognosis
Management is supportive with infection prevention, blood product and fluid support, and treatment of the failing organ systems, ideally with specialist and haematology input
Contamination with radioactive material must be distinguished from irradiation, and decontamination plus staff protection are early priorities
Localised high-dose exposure can cause cutaneous radiation injury with erythema, blistering and later necrosis, sometimes appearing after a delay
reference.pathophysiology: Ionising radiation deposits energy that damages DNA and cellular structures, with the greatest harm to rapidly dividing tissues. Loss of proliferating stem cells in the bone marrow causes pancytopenia, while injury to the intestinal crypt cells breaks down the mucosal barrier, leading to fluid loss, bleeding and sepsis. Very high doses cause vascular and neurological injury. The clinical course reflects the differing turnover rates of these tissues, giving the characteristic phased illness.
additionalDifferentials: Chemotherapy or other cytotoxic drug toxicity
Acute leukaemia or bone marrow failure of other cause
Chemical or toxic exposure causing vomiting
additionalInvestigations: Serial full blood counts with attention to the rate of lymphocyte decline
Estimation of absorbed dose using time to vomiting and available dosimetry
Biological dosimetry such as chromosome aberration analysis where available
Assessment and monitoring for radioactive contamination
Baseline organ function tests and cultures to guide supportive care
redFlags: MEDICAL EMERGENCY: high-dose exposure with very early vomiting, rapidly falling lymphocytes, or neurological or cardiovascular signs indicates severe, potentially fatal illness
Signs of gastrointestinal syndrome with intractable diarrhoea and bleeding
Profound neutropenia with infection or sepsis
Confusion, hypotension or seizures suggesting a very high dose
reference.prognosis: Outcome is strongly dose-dependent: lower doses causing mainly marrow suppression may recover with intensive support, whereas gastrointestinal and neurovascular syndromes from very high doses carry a poor to near-uniformly fatal outlook despite treatment.
pitfalls: Mistaking early prodromal vomiting for simple gastroenteritis
Being reassured by the latent phase and underestimating impending marrow failure
Confusing external irradiation with radioactive contamination and neglecting decontamination
Failing to protect staff and control the scene during care
Not obtaining serial lymphocyte counts for dose estimation
